newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan won't give on sovereignty in islands talks.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan won't give on sovereignty in islands talks.

text.p: Taiwanese negotiators left for Japan on Thursday to discuss fishing rights and other issues arising from a dispute over a chain of East China Sea islands and pledged never to sacrifice Taipei's sovereignty claim.
A seven-member negotiating team from the foreign ministry, interior ministry and Council of Agriculture was to begin talks with Japanese counterparts in Tokyo on Friday.
"The trip is to attend a second round of meetings on fishing rights with Japan," negotiator Lo Kun-tsan told reporters at the airport.
"But I cannot reveal our bottom line at this moment."
Taipei has no diplomatic relations with Tokyo, which recognises Beijing instead. Their extensive economic and social ties are managed by state-funded unofficial agencies.

The meetings, expected to last for one or two days, are the second round since a simmering dispute exploded in July over ownership of the uninhabited islands, which are claimed by Japan as the Senkakus and by Taiwan and China as the Diaoyus.
Fishing rights, not rival claims to the islands themselves, top the agenda as Tokyo -- like Taiwan -- regards its claim of sovereignty to be closed to negotiation.
Lee Chien-chuan, an official at the Council of Agriculture, said Taiwan was not prepared to sacrifice its sovereignty in exchange for fishing rights, state media reported.

Lee was quoted by the state-run Central News Agency as saying Taiwan would seek maximum fishing rights for its people during the talks, but its pre-condition was preservation of Taiwan's sovereignty over the islands.
"We want to make some kind of breakthrough," Lee said.

A right-wing Japanese youth group triggered an angry and increasingly nationalistic backlash from Chinese around Asia after raising Japan's flag and building a lighthouse on the islands in July to assert Tokyo's claim.

Taiwanese fishermen complain that Japanese patrol boats have barred them from fishing near the islands. Japanese patrols also have repulsed boats trying to land protesters from Taiwan and Hong Kong on the islands, deepening anti-Japanese resentment.

Japan took the islands as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895. China and Taiwan say the islands have been Chinese territory for centuries and should have been returned after Japan's World War Two defeat.
